fields.complete_source:
Solution:
Consider a river crossing problem defined by the inputs n, k, and an n-vertex
graph G. There are n passengers to be transported across a river by a pilot, Charon. The
ferry has a maximum capacity of k individuals, which must include Charon to operate the
vessel. The graph G defines conflict constraints: an edge between two vertices indicates
that the corresponding passengers are enemies. The safety conditions dictate that no pair
of enemies may be present together on either riverbank unless Charon is also present at
that location. Prove that the decision problem of determining whether a valid sequence of
crossings exists to transport all n passengers across the river is NP-hard.
To solve the problem of proving that the generalized river crossing problem is NP-hard,
we will formalize the problem in terms of graph theory and relate it to the concept of the
Alcuin number of a graph. We will then use the known complexity results regarding the
Alcuin number and its connection to the Vertex Cover problem.
Problem Formulation
Let the inputs be: - n: the number of passengers (vertices). - k: the capacity of the ferry
(including Charon). Thus, the ferry can carry Charon and at most k −1 passengers. -
G = (V, E): a graph where vertices V represent passengers and edges E represent conflicts.
Rules: 1. Safety: A set of passengers S on a riverbank is safe if and only if either:
- Charon is present at that bank. - Or, S contains no pair of enemies (i.e., S is an In-
dependent Set in G). 2. Crossing: Charon moves between the left bank (L) and the
right bank (R). In each move, Charon takes a subset of passengers P from the current
bank to the other. The size of the group (Charon + passengers) must not exceed k. Thus,
1 ≤|P| + 1 ≤k =⇒0 ≤|P| ≤k −1. 3. Goal: Find a sequence of moves to transport all
passengers from the initial state (V, L) (all passengers at L, Charon at L) to the final state
(∅, R) (no passengers at L, Charon at R).
This problem is deciding whether a valid crossing schedule exists for the given inputs
n, k, G.
Relation to the Alcuin Number
The generalized river crossing problem is studied in combinatorial literature under the name
”Alcuin’s River Crossing Problem”. The minimum boat capacity required to transport a set
of items with conflict graph G is called the Alcuin number of G, denoted by A(G).
The decision problem stated (”Does a valid sequence exist for capacity k?”) is equivalent
to determining whether k ≥A(G).
A schedule consists of a sequence of states. Let St denote the set of passengers remaining
on the left bank L after the t-th crossing. - Initially, S0 = V . - Crossing 1 (L →R):
Charon moves a set P1 to R. S1 = V \ P1. Charon is at R. - Condition: S1 must be an
Independent Set (since Charon is at R). - Capacity: |P1| ≤k −1. - Crossing 2 (R →L):
Charon returns with a set Q1. S2 = S1 ∪Q1. Charon is at L. - Condition: The passengers
left at R, which is V \S2, must be an Independent Set. - Capacity: |Q1| ≤k−1. - In general,
for any odd t (Charon at R), St must be an Independent Set. For any even t (Charon at L),
V \ St must be an Independent Set (which means St is a Vertex Cover).
1

Thus, a solution exists if and only if there is a sequence S0, S1, . . . , Sm such that: 1.
S0 = V, Sm = ∅. 2. St is an Independent Set for odd t. 3. St is a Vertex Cover for even t.
4. |St \ St+1| ≤k −1 for even t (passengers moving L →R). 5. |St+1 \ St| ≤k −1 for odd t
(passengers moving R →L).
Proof of NP-Hardness
We prove that the problem is NP-hard by relating it to the Vertex Cover problem, which
is known to be NP-complete.
Theorem (Prisner 2002, Bahls 2009, Lampis & Mitsou 2011): For any graph G,
the Alcuin number A(G) satisfies:
τ(G) ≤A(G) ≤τ(G) + 1
where τ(G) is the vertex cover number of G (the size of a minimum vertex cover). Further-
more, determining the exact value of A(G) is NP-hard.
Reduction Logic: Consider the first crossing (L →R). Charon must take a set P1
(|P1| ≤k −1) such that the remaining set S1 = V \ P1 is safe. Since Charon will be at R, S1
must be an Independent Set. By definition, if V \ P1 is an Independent Set, then P1 must
be a Vertex Cover. Therefore, a necessary condition for any solution to exist is that G has
a vertex cover of size at most k −1.
∃valid move 1 ⇐⇒τ(G) ≤k −1
This establishes that A(G) ≥τ(G) (if we consider passenger capacity). Specifically, if
the ferry passenger capacity B = k −1 is less than τ(G), no first move is possible.
While the condition τ(G) ≤k −1 is necessary, it is not always sufficient because Charon
must also be able to return and transport the remaining passengers. However, it has been
proven that for general graphs, distinguishing whether the required capacity is equal to τ(G)
or strictly greater is computationally intractable.
Specifically, Lampis and Mitsou (2011) proved that determining if A(G) ≤k is NP-hard.
Since the decision problem ”Does a valid sequence exist?” is exactly ”Is k ≥A(G)?”, the
river crossing problem is NP-hard.
Constructive Argument (Sketch): The hardness effectively stems from the fact that
calculating τ(G) is NP-hard. If we could solve the river crossing decision problem efficiently,
we could solve the Vertex Cover problem. Consider the restricted problem where we ask if
a solution exists with ferry capacity k. If we restrict the number of crossings to exactly 1
(one-way trip), the problem is exactly: ”Does there exist a vertex cover of size ≤k −1?”.
This is the Vertex Cover problem. Although the general problem allows multiple crossings,
the ”bottleneck” of the first move links the capacity directly to the vertex cover number.
The complexity of managing the subsequent return trips for general graphs does not simplify
the problem but rather adds to the complexity (related to the Circular Chromatic Number
of the Kneser graph).
Conclusion
The decision problem of determining whether a valid sequence of crossings exists for an n-
vertex graph G and ferry capacity k is NP-hard. This follows from the equivalence of the
2

problem to determining the Alcuin number of a graph, a known NP-hard problem closely
related to the Vertex Cover problem.
Q.E.D.

fields.explanation: The original K2 has cover {1} of size one and total capacity k=2. Moving both passengers in one crossing needs two passenger seats, so its all-right state cannot follow the all-left state. The headline verifies the Mathlib vertex cover/cardinality and refutes the actual one-crossing transition from state 0 to state 7, retaining its capacity, passenger-origin and bank-safety clauses.
fields.flaw: The proof claims that if the river-crossing problem is restricted to exactly one one-way crossing, it is exactly Vertex Cover: there is a solution iff G has a vertex cover of size at most k−1.

fields.witness:
K2, k=2, exactly one crossing

Use G=K2 with vertices {1,2}, edge (1,2), and ferry capacity k=2, so Charon can carry at most k−1=1 passenger. G has a vertex cover of size 1, e.g. {1}. But with exactly one crossing under the original transport goal, at most one passenger can be moved, leaving the other on the starting bank; hence no one-crossing valid solution reaches the final state. A checker can enumerate the possible one-crossing passenger sets of size ≤1 and verify none equals V.

scope_metadata.final_theorem_status: Not challenged: the NP-hardness theorem is true; only the sketch-level sentence about the exactly-one-crossing restriction is refuted.
scope_metadata.source_kind: Local proof step inside a 'constructive argument (sketch)' of an LLM-written NP-hardness solution (QEDBench); the sentence is a sketch-level misstatement, not the asserted final theorem.
scope_metadata.source_scope: General G and capacity k (Charon plus at most k−1 passengers); the source's own formalization (frozen lines 23–25, 44–47) defines a solution as a schedule from (V, L) to (∅, R), i.e. all passengers moved. The refutation concerns exactly one crossing under that complete-transport goal. A charitable rereading of the sentence as 'a valid first move exists iff τ(G) ≤ k−1' (frozen line 61) would be true and is not refuted.
